```{r}
#| label: setup
library(fda)
library(tidyverse)

evi_raw <- read.csv("data/evi_data.csv")

day_cols    <- names(evi_raw)[str_detect(names(evi_raw), "^Day")]
time_points <- as.numeric(str_remove(day_cols, "^Day"))
evi_mat     <- t(as.matrix(evi_raw[, day_cols]))   # 46 days x 200 locations
dayrng      <- range(time_points)
n_loc       <- ncol(evi_mat)
eval_grid   <- seq(dayrng[1], dayrng[2], length.out = 300)

# Month axis used on every plot
month_days     <- c(1, 32, 60, 91, 121, 152, 182, 213, 244, 274, 305, 335)
add_month_axis <- function(cex = 0.8) {
  axis(1, at = month_days, labels = month.abb, cex.axis = cex)
}

# Helpers for numbers quoted in the text
fmt_lam     <- function(x) format(signif(x, 2), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
pct         <- function(x) format(round(100 * x, 1), nsmall = 1)
day_to_date <- function(d) {
  dt <- as.Date(round(d) - 1, origin = "2025-01-01")
  paste(as.integer(format(dt, "%d")), format(dt, "%B"))
}

col_curve <- rgb(0, 0.45, 0.2, 0.15)
col_green <- "#2c5f2e"

# Bases and roughness penalties
bbasis   <- create.bspline.basis(dayrng, norder = 4, breaks = time_points)  # knot at every reading
fbasis   <- create.fourier.basis(dayrng, nbasis = 45)
curv.Lfd <- int2Lfd(2)                                         # L = D^2
omega    <- 2 * pi / diff(dayrng)
harm.Lfd <- vec2Lfd(c(0, omega^2, 0), rangeval = dayrng)       # L = omega^2 D + D^3

lambdas  <- 10^seq(-4, 6, by = 0.25)
```

```{r}
#| label: smoothing
# Mean GCV across the 200 curves for each lambda
gcv_curve <- function(basis, Lfd) {
  sapply(lambdas, function(lam)
    mean(smooth.basis(time_points, evi_mat, fdPar(basis, Lfd, lam))$gcv))
}
gcv_d2 <- gcv_curve(bbasis, curv.Lfd)
gcv_ha <- gcv_curve(fbasis, harm.Lfd)

lambda_d2 <- lambdas[which.min(gcv_d2)]
lambda_ha <- lambdas[which.min(gcv_ha)]

sm_d2 <- smooth.basis(time_points, evi_mat, fdPar(bbasis, curv.Lfd, lambda_d2))
sm_ha <- smooth.basis(time_points, evi_mat, fdPar(fbasis, harm.Lfd, lambda_ha))

smooth_d2 <- eval.fd(eval_grid, sm_d2$fd)
smooth_ha <- eval.fd(eval_grid, sm_ha$fd)
mean_ha   <- rowMeans(smooth_ha)

# Derivatives of the harmonic-penalty smooth
D1      <- eval.fd(eval_grid, sm_ha$fd, Lfdobj = 1)
D2      <- eval.fd(eval_grid, sm_ha$fd, Lfdobj = 2)
mean_D1 <- rowMeans(D1)

peak_day     <- eval_grid[which.max(mean_ha)]
greenup_day  <- eval_grid[which.max(mean_D1)]
browning_day <- eval_grid[which.min(mean_D1)]
winter_level <- mean(mean_ha[eval_grid <= 90])
peak_level   <- max(mean_ha)
```

```{r}
#| label: fpca
# Unpenalised functional PCA
nharm    <- 10
pca_unpn <- pca.fd(sm_ha$fd, nharm = nharm)
varprop  <- pca_unpn$varprop
n_80     <- which(cumsum(varprop) >= 0.80)[1]

# Smoothed PCA: choose the penalty by 10-fold cross-validation.
# For each lambda, fit on 9/10 of the curves, rebuild the unseen 1/10 from
# K components (least-squares scores), and add up what the components miss.
set.seed(2026)
K           <- 3
folds       <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = n_loc))
pca_lambdas <- c(0, 10^seq(-2, 6, by = 1))          # 0 = no penalty
cv_error    <- numeric(length(pca_lambdas))

for (j in seq_along(pca_lambdas)) {
  for (f in 1:10) {
    train <- which(folds != f)
    test  <- which(folds == f)
    pca_j <- pca.fd(sm_ha$fd[train], nharm = K,
                    harmfdPar = fdPar(bbasis, curv.Lfd, pca_lambdas[j]))
    mu_j  <- as.vector(eval.fd(eval_grid, pca_j$meanfd))
    H     <- eval.fd(eval_grid, pca_j$harmonics)       # 300 x K component shapes
    X     <- smooth_ha[, test] - mu_j                   # unseen curves, centred
    S     <- solve(crossprod(H), crossprod(H, X))      # best-fitting scores
    cv_error[j] <- cv_error[j] + sum((X - H %*% S)^2)
  }
}
# Keep no penalty unless some penalty cuts the error by more than 1%
best_gain  <- 1 - min(cv_error) / cv_error[pca_lambdas == 0]
#lambda_pca <- if (best_gain < 0.01) 0 else pca_lambdas[which.min(cv_error)]
lambda_pca <- if (best_gain <= 0.01) 0 else pca_lambdas[which.min(cv_error)]

pca_sm     <- pca.fd(sm_ha$fd, nharm = nharm,
                     harmfdPar = fdPar(bbasis, curv.Lfd, lambda_pca))
varprop_sm <- pca_sm$varprop
n_80_sm    <- which(cumsum(varprop_sm) >= 0.80)[1]

flat_max <- max(pca_lambdas[cv_error <= 1.01 * min(cv_error)])   # within 1% of the best

pca_verdict <- if (lambda_pca == 0) {
  paste0("Cross-validation found no benefit from smoothing the components: no penalty ",
         "and penalties up to $\\lambda$ = ", fmt_lam(flat_max), " rebuild held-out curves ",
         "equally well, and larger penalties make the reconstruction worse, so the components ",
         "were left unpenalised. Because the curves were already smoothed before this step, ",
         "this tests the penalty on the components given that smoothing, not the whole ",
         "workflow. Heavier penalties would flatten sharp features such as the May peak in ",
         "the third component, so the result is consistent with that feature reflecting real ",
         "differences in green-up timing between locations, though it does not prove it, and ",
         "eight-day sampling limits how precisely that timing can be resolved.")
} else {
  paste0("Cross-validation picked $\\lambda$ = ", fmt_lam(lambda_pca), ". At that level ",
         "the components are smoother, and the share of variation explained by the first ",
         "three moves from ", pct(sum(varprop[1:3])), "% (unpenalised) to ",
         pct(sum(varprop_sm[1:3])), "%.")
}
```

## Summary

Satellite readings of vegetation greenness at `r n_loc` locations were treated as `r n_loc` smooth curves, one per location, so that the shape of each growing season could be analysed rather than 46 separate numbers.

- **The typical year.** The average location sits at an EVI of about `r round(winter_level, 2)` through winter, greens up fastest around **`r day_to_date(greenup_day)`**, peaks around `r day_to_date(peak_day)` at about `r round(peak_level, 2)`, and fades fastest around **`r day_to_date(browning_day)`**.
- **How locations differ.** Three components explain **`r pct(sum(varprop_sm[1:3]))`%** of the differences between locations: the height of the summer peak (`r pct(varprop_sm[1])`%), how green a location stays in winter (`r pct(varprop_sm[2])`%), and the timing of green-up (`r pct(varprop_sm[3])`%).
- **How the settings were chosen.** Smoothing levels were chosen by generalised cross-validation, and the penalty on the components by 10-fold cross-validation on curves held out from the fit.

## 1. Introduction

The Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) is a satellite measure of how green and dense vegetation is: higher values mean more active, leafy vegetation. Measured every eight days, it traces out each location's growing season.

Treating the 46 readings as one curve per location makes it possible to ask questions about the *shape* of the season:

1.  What does a typical growing season look like?
2.  When does vegetation green up and fade fastest?
3.  In what main ways do locations differ from one another?

## 2. Data

The data hold `r length(time_points)` readings per location, every eight days from day `r dayrng[1]` to day `r dayrng[2]` of a single year, for `r n_loc` locations. There are no missing values. Readings range from `r round(min(evi_mat), 2)` to `r round(max(evi_mat), 2)`. No information is available on where the locations are or what vegetation grows there.

```{r}
#| label: fig-raw
#| fig-cap: "Raw EVI readings for all 200 locations (green) and their mean (black)."
#| fig-height: 3.6
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.5, 0.8), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.82)
matplot(time_points, evi_mat, type = "l", lty = 1, col = col_curve,
        xlab = "", ylab = "EVI", xaxt = "n", bty = "l")
add_month_axis()
lines(time_points, rowMeans(evi_mat), lwd = 2.2)
```

Every location follows the same broad pattern (@fig-raw): flat and low in winter, a steep rise in May, a summer plateau, and a steep fall in October. Locations differ most in the height of the summer plateau and in their winter baseline.

## 3. Methods

**Smoothing.** Each location's readings $y_1,\dots,y_{46}$ were turned into a smooth curve $x(t)$ by minimising a penalised sum of squares,

$$\sum_{j=1}^{46}\big(y_j - x(t_j)\big)^2 + \lambda \int \big[Lx(t)\big]^2\,dt ,$$

where the first term rewards fitting the readings, the second penalises roughness, and $\lambda$ sets the balance. Two penalties were compared:

- **Curvature**, $L = D^2$, with a cubic B-spline basis and a knot at every reading. This penalises all bending equally.
- **Harmonic acceleration**, $L = \omega^2 D + D^3$ with $\omega = 2\pi/T$, using a Fourier basis. Constants, $\sin \omega t$ and $\cos \omega t$ all satisfy $Lx = 0$, so a pure annual cycle costs nothing and only departures from it are penalised. This suits data whose main signal is a yearly rhythm.

For both, $\lambda$ was chosen by minimising the mean generalised cross-validation (GCV) score across the 200 curves.

**Rates of change.** The first and second derivatives of the harmonic-penalty curves give the speed of greening and how that speed changes.

**Functional principal component analysis (FPCA).** FPCA finds the component curves $\xi_k(t)$ along which locations vary most, so that each curve is approximately the mean plus a weighted sum of a few components. A smoothed version (Silverman's method) chooses each component to maximise

$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}\left(\int \xi(t)\,x_i(t)\,dt\right)}{\int \xi(t)^2\,dt + \lambda \int \big[D^2\xi(t)\big]^2\,dt},$$

so a larger $\lambda$ gives smoother components. Here $\lambda$ was chosen by **10-fold cross-validation**: for each candidate, the components were fitted on nine tenths of the curves, the remaining tenth were rebuilt from the first three components by least squares, and the squared reconstruction error was summed. The candidates included $\lambda = 0$ (no penalty), and a penalty was used only if it cut the error by more than 1% compared with no penalty. The curves were smoothed before this step, so this tests the penalty on the components given that smoothing, not the whole workflow.

## 4. Results

### 4.1 Smoothing

```{r}
#| label: fig-smooth
#| fig-cap: "Smoothed curves under each penalty, with the GCV-chosen smoothing parameter."
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 2, 0.8), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8)
matplot(eval_grid, smooth_d2, type = "l", lty = 1, col = col_curve,
        xlab = "", ylab = "EVI", xaxt = "n", bty = "l",
        main = bquote("Curvature penalty," ~ lambda == .(fmt_lam(lambda_d2))),
        cex.main = 0.9, font.main = 1)
add_month_axis(); lines(eval_grid, rowMeans(smooth_d2), lwd = 2)
matplot(eval_grid, smooth_ha, type = "l", lty = 1, col = col_curve,
        xlab = "", ylab = "EVI", xaxt = "n", bty = "l",
        main = bquote("Harmonic acceleration," ~ lambda == .(fmt_lam(lambda_ha))),
        cex.main = 0.9, font.main = 1)
add_month_axis(); lines(eval_grid, mean_ha, lwd = 2)
```

GCV chose $\lambda$ = `r fmt_lam(lambda_d2)` for the curvature penalty (effective degrees of freedom `r round(sm_d2$df, 1)`) and $\lambda$ = `r fmt_lam(lambda_ha)` for the harmonic acceleration penalty (`r round(sm_ha$df, 1)`). Both reproduce the seasonal shape closely (@fig-smooth), with minimum mean GCV scores of `r format(signif(min(gcv_d2), 3), scientific = FALSE)` and `r format(signif(min(gcv_ha), 3), scientific = FALSE)`. The harmonic penalty does this with fewer effective degrees of freedom, because the annual cycle it leaves unpenalised already accounts for most of each curve. The rest of the analysis uses the harmonic-penalty curves. The GCV curves are in the appendix (@fig-gcv).

### 4.2 When greening is fastest

```{r}
#| label: fig-deriv
#| fig-cap: "First derivative (speed of greening, left) and second derivative (change in that speed, right). Bold lines are averages across locations; dashed lines mark the fastest green-up and the fastest decline."
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.6, 0.8, 0.8), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8)
matplot(eval_grid, D1, type = "l", lty = 1, col = rgb(0, 0.3, 0.7, 0.12),
        xlab = "", ylab = "Change in EVI per day", xaxt = "n", bty = "l")
add_month_axis(); abline(h = 0, col = "grey50")
lines(eval_grid, mean_D1, col = "navy", lwd = 2)
abline(v = c(greenup_day, browning_day), lty = 2, col = "grey30")
matplot(eval_grid, D2, type = "l", lty = 1, col = rgb(0.6, 0.1, 0, 0.12),
        xlab = "", ylab = "Second derivative", xaxt = "n", bty = "l")
add_month_axis(); abline(h = 0, col = "grey50")
lines(eval_grid, rowMeans(D2), col = "darkred", lwd = 2)
```

The first derivative is the speed of change in greenness (@fig-deriv, left). It is close to zero through winter and summer, when greenness is stable. It has a sharp positive peak at the fastest green-up, around **`r day_to_date(greenup_day)`**, and a sharp negative trough at the fastest decline, around **`r day_to_date(browning_day)`**. Where it crosses zero, greenness is at a turning point: the summer peak, around `r day_to_date(peak_day)`, or the winter low. The second derivative (right) is largest just before and after each of these extremes, marking where the season switches on and off.

### 4.3 How locations differ

```{r}
#| label: fig-scree
#| fig-cap: "Share of the variation between locations explained by each component, and the cumulative share."
#| fig-height: 3
par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 0.5, 0.8), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8)
plot(1:nharm, 100 * varprop_sm, type = "b", pch = 19, col = col_green,
     ylim = c(0, 100), xlab = "Component", ylab = "% of variation", bty = "l")
lines(1:nharm, 100 * cumsum(varprop_sm), type = "b", pch = 17, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
abline(h = 80, lty = 3, col = "red")
legend("right", c("Each component", "Cumulative", "80%"),
       col = c(col_green, "grey40", "red"), lty = c(1, 2, 3), pch = c(19, 17, NA),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

The first `r n_80_sm` components together explain `r pct(sum(varprop_sm[1:n_80_sm]))`% of the variation (@fig-scree). Each one is easiest to read by adding and subtracting two standard deviations of it from the mean curve (@fig-pcs).

```{r}
#| label: fig-pcs
#| fig-cap: "Effect of each of the first three components: the mean curve (black) plus (red) and minus (blue) two standard deviations of the component."
#| fig-height: 3.2
mean_pc <- as.vector(eval.fd(eval_grid, pca_sm$meanfd))
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.75)
for (k in 1:3) {
  fpc_k <- as.vector(eval.fd(eval_grid, pca_sm$harmonics[k]))
  sd_k  <- sqrt(pca_sm$values[k])
  plot(eval_grid, mean_pc, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "", ylab = "EVI",
       xaxt = "n", bty = "l", cex.main = 0.95,
       main = paste0("Component ", k, " (", pct(varprop_sm[k]), "%)"),
       ylim = range(mean_pc + 2 * sd_k * fpc_k, mean_pc - 2 * sd_k * fpc_k))
  add_month_axis(0.65)
  lines(eval_grid, mean_pc + 2 * sd_k * fpc_k, col = "#8b1a1a", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  lines(eval_grid, mean_pc - 2 * sd_k * fpc_k, col = "navy",    lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
}
```

- **Component 1 (`r pct(varprop_sm[1])`%): height of the summer peak.** It moves the summer plateau up or down while leaving winter almost unchanged. It separates locations with lush summers from those with sparser summer vegetation.
- **Component 2 (`r pct(varprop_sm[2])`%): winter greenness.** It moves the winter baseline, from January to April and from November to December, with the summer plateau almost unchanged. It separates locations that stay relatively green through winter from those that drop to a low baseline.
- **Component 3 (`r pct(varprop_sm[3])`%): timing.** It mainly shifts the May green-up earlier or later, with a smaller opposite change in late summer. It captures *when* in the season greenness arrives rather than how much of it there is.

### 4.4 Does smoothing the components help?

```{r}
#| label: fig-cv
#| fig-cap: "Left: 10-fold cross-validation error for the penalty on the components. Right: the third component without a penalty (grey) and at the chosen penalty (green)."
h_un <- as.vector(eval.fd(eval_grid, pca_unpn$harmonics[3]))
h_sm <- as.vector(eval.fd(eval_grid, pca_sm$harmonics[3]))
if (sum(h_un * h_sm) < 0) h_sm <- -h_sm               # component signs are arbitrary
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.6, 0.8, 0.8), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8)
x_pos      <- seq_along(pca_lambdas)                   # even spacing, so 0 can be shown
lam_labels <- ifelse(pca_lambdas == 0, "0", paste0("1e", log10(pca_lambdas)))
plot(x_pos, cv_error, type = "b", pch = 19, col = col_green, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "CV reconstruction error", bty = "l")
axis(1, at = x_pos, labels = lam_labels, cex.axis = 0.7)
abline(v = x_pos[pca_lambdas == lambda_pca], lty = 2, col = "red")
plot(eval_grid, h_un, type = "l", col = "grey50", lwd = 1.5, xlab = "",
     ylab = "Component 3", xaxt = "n", bty = "l", ylim = range(h_un, h_sm))
lines(eval_grid, h_sm, col = col_green, lwd = 2)
add_month_axis(); abline(h = 0, col = "grey80")
```

`r pca_verdict` Without a penalty, the first three components explain `r pct(sum(varprop[1:3]))`% of the variation (@fig-cv).

## 5. Limitations

- **One year only.** The data cover a single season, so the analysis says nothing about how locations change from year to year.
- **No location information.** Without coordinates or land-cover types, the components describe patterns but cannot be linked to causes, such as evergreen versus deciduous vegetation or altitude.
- **Eight-day readings.** Green-up takes only two or three readings, so its estimated timing is only as precise as the sampling allows.
- **Periodic basis.** The Fourier basis assumes the year joins up at the end. This is reasonable here, because January and December levels are similar, but it would mislead for a year with an overall trend.
- **Grid choices.** Smoothing parameters were chosen from a grid, and three components were kept by an 80% rule rather than a formal test.

## 6. Conclusion

Across `r n_loc` locations, vegetation follows one clear seasonal rhythm: a quiet winter, a sharp green-up around `r day_to_date(greenup_day)`, a summer plateau and a sharp decline around `r day_to_date(browning_day)`. Locations differ in three main ways: how green the summer gets, how green the winter stays, and when the season starts. Together these account for `r pct(sum(varprop_sm[1:3]))`% of the differences. Each method choice, the smoothing level and the penalty on the components, was made by cross-validation rather than by eye.

## Appendix

```{r}
#| label: fig-gcv
#| fig-cap: "Mean GCV score against the smoothing parameter for each penalty; the dashed line marks the minimum."
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.6, 2, 0.8), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8)
plot(lambdas, gcv_d2, log = "x", type = "b", pch = 19, cex = 0.45, col = col_green,
     xlab = expression(lambda ~ "(log scale)"), ylab = "Mean GCV", bty = "l",
     main = "Curvature penalty", cex.main = 0.9, font.main = 1)
abline(v = lambda_d2, lty = 2, col = "red")
plot(lambdas, gcv_ha, log = "x", type = "b", pch = 19, cex = 0.45, col = col_green,
     xlab = expression(lambda ~ "(log scale)"), ylab = "Mean GCV", bty = "l",
     main = "Harmonic acceleration penalty", cex.main = 0.9, font.main = 1)
abline(v = lambda_ha, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

**Reproducing this report.** Every number in this report is calculated when the document is rendered. The source is `evi_fda.qmd`, and it needs R with the `fda` and `tidyverse` packages. The analysis began as a course project for Functional Data Analysis at the University of Glasgow (2026). This version adds cross-validated smoothing of the components and a full write-up.
